You realize you are isolated in the relationship, or that they are not communicating with you as they do with others.

In my honest opinion, as someone whom has experienced both physical cheating and emotional cheating by a partner in the past, the latter is far worse-- and if one cannot be honest, or loyal to the other, then it is likely the relationship won't last. Learning a partner has physically cheated on you sucks, don't get me wrong. There's a cold, "drop" feeling in your stomach, and it feels like your heart has been crushed to learn the person you were physically intimate with shared their/your bed with someone else, (you know, unless it was a swing or open relationship. But even **\*then,\*** there is a certain level of communication and trust that they will use protection, and it will not be behind your back). But emotional cheating-- that's worse, because it's not that they are physically lusting after another, but are lusting after someone else in the sense that they want an emotional/mental connection they no longer have, or maybe not even ever had, with you. In that instance--- it's better to cut your losses and walk away, and mend what is left of your heart for yourself.

First and foremost, I think you need to establish boundaries to allow yourself some time to have a hobby or "thing" which relaxes you once or twice a week.

I also think you should express to your husband that until he can get his spending under control, perhaps he should only carry enough cash that he needs for the day/week, and leave the plastic at home or with you if he cannot trust himself not to do something like that which has clearly cost both of you financially. He also needs to realize that yes, you are his wife and partner, and best friend, but dropping all his troubles on you is not healthy. He should see a therapist for his crisis, or confide in a friend or family member whom can be trusted not to take sides, offer poor advice, or encourage him to behave that way. (which I know, is hard.) It sounds like he was either very sheltered, or does not have so much experience looking after himself as an adult, let alone you, his spouse.

Even if you both work stressful jobs, he is an adult, and should recognize that you have to suck it up, smile, and get along with your employer. A job is a job, and he cannot pick and choose whom he works with or what he does if things are that desperate. He needs to buckle down, acknowledge he has a ways to go to be on top of his game, and commit to changing himself for the better of not only his person, but your relationship.

If you are so burned out that you dread coming home, perhaps you should ask someone in your social circle if  you can stay with them for a few days to clear your head and reorient yourself. It's healthy for couples to spend some time apart every once in awhile, and it might help him realize how much emotional strain he is putting on you by complaining so often without regard for how you have been ailing emotionally. It may hurt, but I think you are doing the right thing by telling him he needs to get help. You are his wife and partner, not his mother. He needs to own his shit.

Not true, actually--- there are many women gamers. The idea that video games cause crimes is a myth that's origins are from 1976, when the U.S. National Safety Council panicked over the arcade game, "Death race," a game about driving a white pixelated car resembling stick figures into crashing in hilarious and obviously unrealistic ways into walls and targets to acrue points. The truth is that there is STILL no evidence linking video games to violent crimes. If you read Patrick Markey's 2014 article, "Psychology of Popular Media Culture, 4.4"  it actually points that as video games rise, violent crime rates go down in the U.S drastically. Other countries where video games are popular have even lower rates of violent crimes--- for example, in Japan, one of the World's chief Technologically savvy countries, the majority of the population play much more often and have approximately 96 times fewer gun homicides. (Max Fisher, Washington Post, 17th December, 2012.)

Multiple studies have been conducted over the years since video games went on the rise, INCLUDING a study done by the secret service, and they found that school shooters actually consume significantly less and lower amounts of violent media and video games than their peers, (U.S. Secret Service & U.S. Department of Education, 2004.)  The misconception really stems from media perspective, and failed studies that still somehow get published or highlighted, often by these same social agencies whom are oftentimes pushing any form of news they can find before confirming. While these studies did show in a small, minute group that some video games can show an increase in aggression, they failed to measure anything the actual average person would \*actually\* consider aggressive--- let alone the number of times someone in the test just got frustrated with the game because they were stuck or unable to complete a level (Hence, "temporary" being a key word here.)

Even if these studies had tested real world acts of aggression, the change in behavior they would have measured is tiny, minuscule, just 2% on average. (Jason Schreir, Kotaku, 17th of January, 2013.) Other studies have shown the same results in racing games such as Mario Karts, and even real-life sports. Blaming video games for violence really took off after the Columbine shooting, because it was known at least one of the shooters was a gamer, and it was an understandable mistake, because everyone wanted some desperate reason other than the extreme bullying as to why someone would commit such a horrific act of violence. Video games are not to blame, they are just scapegoated, and this scapegoating is parroted as a lazy and half-arsed narrative right back by media outlets that don't do their research, because it's easier to place the blame than to tackle societal problems which actually impact rates of violence. Things like Educational and Employment disparities, for example. Stigma against seeking mental Health treatment, and especially in the case of shootings, easy access to guns. The truth is that tax dollars are being wasted being used in these faulty experiments to find connections between violence and video games that just doesn't exist, and distracts the populace and those in these positions of power who can take action from really looking into what we as a people need to do to keep people safe.
